SYMPTOM_TEXT: Persistent serosanguinous draining ulcer/The blister transformed into an ulcer over the next few days; Radiation recall phenomenon; On her 12th fraction, she developed a blister on her right thigh; Serosanguinous drainage; This literature report (initial receipt date: 27-Jul-2026) concerns an elderly female patient.   The female patient with a medical history of low-grade liposarcoma of the right thigh underwent resection in 2009, followed by a local recurrence treated with a second resection in 2010 and adjuvant radiation therapy (50 Gy in 25 fractions, plus a 10 Gy boost). In 2021, she presented with another local recurrence of dedifferentiated liposarcoma in the right thigh, leading to further surgical resection without adjuvant treatment. The pathology revealed dedifferentiated liposarcoma, pT4N0, grade 3.  In –2023, During surveillance, a chest CT scan revealed a prominent axillary node, leading to a mammogram that identified a 7 mm invasive lobular carcinoma (ILC) of the right breast, grade 2, Estrogen Receptor/Progesterone Receptor (ER/PR) positive, Human Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor 2 (HER2) negative, with Kiel 67 (Ki-67) of 20% (cT1bN0M0). She subsequently underwent a right lumpectomy and sentinel lymph node biopsy, showing pT1bN0, ILC with negative margins.   The patient received hypo-fractionated whole-breast radiation (40.05 Gy in 15 fractions, followed by a 10 Gy boost). The patient did not receive any systemic chemotherapy during the observed period, nor any therapeutic drugs known to cause Radiation recall phenomenon (RRP).   On her 12th fraction, she developed a blister on her right thigh, associated with serosanguinous drainage. This blister resembled a reaction during her earlier sarcoma radiation in 2010. Investigation revealed that she had received Moderna's COVID-19, RSV, and influenza vaccines for influenza vaccination (INN Flu Vaccine Seasonal: route of administration, dose, anatomical location, batch number, expiry date, trade name and manufacturer: not reported- to be requested upon follow up) three days earlier.  The blister transformed into an ulcer over the next few days. The ulcer base contained pink granulation, slough, and necrotic or devitalized tissue with exposed subcutaneous tissue and no signs of infection. The ulcer resolved with wound care after two months. Importantly, the patient's pre-existing grade 1 radiation dermatitis in the breast did not worsen after vaccination.  Author's comment: Radiation recall phenomenon (RRP) is a rare and unpredictable reaction characterized by the reactivation of inflammatory responses in previously irradiated tissues upon exposure to a triggering agent. In this case, the patient exhibited a maculopapular rash in the irradiated regions and a persistent serosanguinous draining ulcer in an area treated with radiation a decade earlier. Interestingly, the patient's radiation-induced grade 1 dermatitis in the breast did not worsen following vaccination, suggesting that the phenomenon may exhibit a differential response based on the timing of radiation therapy and individual tissue susceptibility.   The occurrence of RRP following vaccination in our patient offers important insights for counselling future patients with radiation history. While our case does not provide definitive evidence to recommend delaying radiation treatment following vaccination, since RRP occurred only in the previously irradiated field while sparing the active treatment site, clinicians should consider several practical approaches.; Reporter's Comments: Causality: Due to the spontaneous nature of the case, events are considered related for reporting purposes. However, patient's history of blister during earlier sarcoma radiation/adjuvant radiation therapy provides more plausible/alternative explanation for events skin ulcer, blister, radiation recall phenomena, and secretion discharge attributed to skin ulcer and blister. Of note, concomitant administration of COVID-19 and respiratory syncytial virus vaccines considered as confounders/trigger factors for the events.

Initially, patient experienced random black-out events while standing or walking ? a complete black that would cause her to fall to the floor.  Over time, the frequency of these fainting episodes increased until she was fainting every day, sometimes multiple times per day.  In conjunction with this increase in frequency, she also developed other symptoms: sudden spikes in her resting heart rate (at times, over 200 bpm), headaches, intestinal discomfort, and sudden swings from feeling cold to feeling flush and hot. Over four cardiologists have thoroughly evaluated patient?s heart.  At one point, she wore a heart monitor for several weeks that recorded multiple severe episodes.  All cardiologists declared her heart to be fine, but said something outside of her heart was triggering the heart?s sinus node.  Multiple neurologists theorized that the autonomic portion of patient?s brain was misfiring.  Upon multiple recommendations from doctors, patient participated in the Protocol Physical Therapy program for a year and half.  In her first session, they put her on a recumbent bike at low speed and low resistance, and she blacked out after 12 minutes.  On December 3, 2025, patient?s heart rate spiked to 205 bpm for several minutes as she was gathering items from her room for a shower.  Then her heart rate suddenly dropped to 40 bpm, and she had an immediate onset of the following symptoms:  level 8-out-of-10 headache, trouble breathing (as if an elephant was on her chest), extreme dizziness (but no fainting), extreme nausea (but no vomiting), extremely hot and sweaty (no temp, but skin hot to the touch), cold and clammy hands, severe muscle weakness (despite being an active hockey player).  As I drove her to the ER, her processing speed in understanding and responding to questions drastically plummeted.  Full-body shivering began 30 minutes after the initial onset of symptoms.  Within an hour, and after 30 seconds of being placed on an ER bed, patient lost consciousness and quit breathing for approximately 30 minutes.  She immediately received bagged oxygen until she started breathing on her own again.  She was admitted to the hospital and the next morning revealed an alarming lack of muscle strength (she failed the neurological examination, unable to resist any pushing or pulling of her arms and legs), her processing speed was still excessively slow (taking three times to understand the question: are you having any pain?), and she required two nurses to get to the restroom and back due to her severe dizziness.  Days later, we discovered evidence of memory loss (not remembering anything she had done or said) and extreme difficulty in processing basic math questions or pulling a single sentence together.  Her recovery took months, and she still does not feel like she has fully regained her normal mental processing speed.  She had two more episodes similar to the December 3 episode (loss of consciousness, cessation of breathing, etc.) on February 17, 2026.  On March, 26, 2026, via a tilt table test performed by Dr. at the Hospital, patient was diagnosed with Postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS).  Ancestrally, patient?s parents? and family ancestors have no similar conditions.

Patient and Pharmacist discussed the vaccine, pharmacist warned this one stings, patient watched and noticed the stinging, complained it was still stinging for about 10 seconds, then fainted. He became verbal again and he said this has happened before, blood pressure  was 112/64 with pulse 62.   Over the next 20 minutes, patient was given water, a Gatorade, and he remained with feet up, eyes closed, but verbal. He asked to use the restroom and we had male vision center manager walk him to the bathroom as a safety measure. When he returned, Patient said he did have breakfast (sausage burrito) shortly beforehand. He said he has has a rare vasovagal response to needles sight of blood (after he felt better).   The pre-vaccine questionnaire did not reveal this.   I suggested he find a hotel and not drive for 24 hours or until he feels 100% normal.  He agreed that might be a good idea.  He went to the restaurant with his laptop to look into that.    2 hours later he returned to the pharmacy to tell me he took a nap in his car (with the A/C on) and some food and fells 100% better.

Received my second Pfizer-BioNTech COVID-19 vaccination on 04/08/2021, lot EW0153. I had no prior history of seizures. On 05/08/2021 at approximately 8:00 PM, 30 days after vaccination, my wife witnessed me experience a generalized tonic-clonic seizure while I was sitting at my computer. She later reported approximately 90 seconds of convulsions with my eyes rolling upward, followed by loss of consciousness and heavy snoring. I had a small amount of urinary incontinence and no tongue biting. I had no warning or premonitory symptoms. Paramedics were called and I was evaluated in the emergency department.  CT of the head was negative and my neurological examination was normal afterward. Laboratory testing did not identify an electrolyte abnormality or other obvious provoking cause, and drug screening was negative. The emergency physician classified the seizure as idiopathic. I was not started on antiseizure medication. Neurology later documented that there was no identified precipitating factor. Subsequent brain MRI did not identify a structural seizure focus, and EEG showed no epileptiform discharges or seizures. I have not experienced another known seizure since that event.  However, since the seizure I have experienced cognitive and neurological changes that I did not have before. I have increasing difficulty remembering names and connecting people's faces with their names, including people I know. My ability to retain and recall information has also noticeably declined. One example is remembering mathematical formulas and other information that I previously would have been able to learn and retain; I now have significant difficulty recalling formulas even after studying them. I have also experienced problems with attention, awareness, and/or spatial judgment, including several accidents or incidents in a parking garage that were unusual for me compared with how I functioned before the seizure.  I reported these cognitive concerns to a doctor a couple of years after the seizure, but no neurological or cognitive follow-up evaluation was performed, and I did not raise the issue again afterward. These problems have continued.  I am reporting this event because my first-ever generalized tonic-clonic seizure occurred 30 days after my second Pfizer-BioNTech COVID-19 vaccination, followed by persistent cognitive changes that were not present beforehand. I cannot establish whether the vaccination caused the seizure or the subsequent cognitive problems, but I believe the complete sequence and continuing symptoms should be documented and evaluated.
LAB_DATA: 05/08-05/09/2021 Emergency Department evaluation: CT head without contrast was negative for intracranial hemorrhage, mass, infarct, or other acute abnormality. EKG showed normal sinus rhythm with no arrhythmia. Laboratory testing was largely unremarkable with sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.4 mmol/L, calcium 8.7 mg/dL, magnesium 1.7 mg/dL, and glucose 116 mg/dL. TSH was elevated at 8.275 mcIU/mL with normal free T4 of 1.1 ng/dL. Urine drug screen was negative for amphetamines, cocaine, cannabinoids, opiates, benzodiazepines, barbiturates, PCP, and methadone. No electrolyte or other clear metabolic cause for the seizure was identified. 06/30/2021 brain MRI using seizure protocol showed no acute infarction or hemorrhage and no structural seizure focus; hippocampi were symmetric. MRI did note spontaneous T1 signal in the bilateral globus pallidi with recommendation for clinical/laboratory correlation. 08/12/2021 EEG showed mild nonspecific nonepileptiform abnormalities, greatest over the left temporal region and minimal over the right temporal region. No epileptiform discharges and no seizures were recorded.

He was answering questions appropriately and stated his head hurt and that he felt dizzy. Staff slowly sat him up, moved him onto an exam table to rest. He was continually attached to vital machine and his pulse, O2 and blood pressure remained normal. He was pale and continued complaining of headache so the office staff did call EMS. He was taken to the local ER.

SYMPTOM_TEXT: Went to supper and was walking around store.  She started having vision problems and stated that she was feeling very tired all of a sudden.  We continued to walk around the store for about 5-10 more minutes when she started shaking uncontrollably.  We said her name and she just repeated "I'm fine" over and over, but we then said her name repeatedly and she did almost appeared catatonic.  My husband was holding her up and I think that she would have collapsed if he had not been holding onto her.  An employee called for an ambulance as she was "seizing" or shaking or whatever.  The episode lasted about 2-3 minutes or so.  It then passed and she said that her vision was back to normal and she didn't feel tired anymore.  We then walked to the front of the store to wait for the ambulance.  We waited for awhile, but she seemed fine and the ambulance was nowhere to be seen, so we left for home.  At home, I checked her pupils were dilating, no temperature, blood pressure was normal, so after pushing a bunch of fluids, I slept on the coach to watch her overnight.  I woke her several times and she appeared to be fine even the next morning.  She later said that leading up to the event, the vision problems were like tunnel vision and she was having stabbing pains in her head.  She also said that when she was actually shaking, she felt her heart racing.  When she was not responding to my husband calling her name, she said that she could hear him, but she thought that she was answering him.  She called in sick to her job as a lifeguard on Friday, just to be on the safe side because she didn't want anything to happen to her while she was guarding.  I called into the health department and spoke with the nurse who administered her hepatitis B vaccine the day before to tell him what happened and after he said that as long as she appeared okay now, that I should just watch her closely and to report the adverse reaction at this website.  She has since been having a few random headaches since then, but appears to be okay.

This case was associated with a product complaint.   On an unknown date, the patient received Penmenvy. On an unknown date, an unknown time after receiving Penmenvy, the patient experienced occupational exposure while preparing product for administration (Verbatim: Accidental exposure while preparing drug for administration), inadvertent exposure to vaccine (Verbatim: Accidental exposure while preparing drug for administration), device plunger issue (Verbatim: plunger came out) and pharmaceutical product complaint (Verbatim: Product quality complaint). The outcome of the occupational exposure while preparing product for administration, inadvertent exposure to vaccine, device plunger issue and pharmaceutical product complaint were not applicable.   It was unknown if the reporter considered the device plunger issue to be related to Penmenvy and Penmenvy Pre-Filled Syringe Device.  This report is made by GSK without prejudice and does not imply any admission or liability for the incident or its consequences.   Additional Information: GSK receipt date: 05-AUG-2026 Three nurses from the office informed the reporter of a Penmenvy complaint and were present during the call to provide details. This was the first time the office had used Penmenvy. The customer confirmed that all preparation and handling steps had been performed according to instructions before the potential product quality complaint (PQC) was identified. The suspect product was not available for return to GSK because the components had been discarded before GSK was contacted, and no photographs were taken. The customer reported having vaccine product from two different cartons; therefore, two separate PQCs were filed. This case pertains to one dose from Carton #1, Lot 7J5LF, containing components ABHE81A and AMEMA023B (lyophilized vial, Material #708575), and was associated with an adverse event (AE). A separate case was filed for two suspect doses from Carton #2, Lot 55ZX7, containing components ABHE80A and AMEMA022A (lyophilized vial, Material #708054), with no associated AE. The office confirmed that all operations had been performed appropriately prior to discovery of the defect. Because the vaccine was new to the practice, a GSK Vaccine Representative had instructed staff and guided them through the first reconstitution procedure. All staff members had received Penmenvy-specific training. On three separate occasions during vaccine preparation, the plunger became difficult to push after insertion into the vial. Subsequently, the entire plunger assembly, including both the rod and stopper, detached and fell completely out of the syringe barrel. The defect was discovered during vaccine preparation and reconstitution. The affected product was not administered to a patient. The complaint involved the pre-filled syringe component. Further investigation revealed that the entire plunger assembly detached during use while staff attempted to push the liquid contents from the pre-filled syringe into the vial for reconstitution. The plunger was unusable once the issue occurred. No blockages were observed within the syringe barrel, and no abnormal particles were noted in the vaccine. A Luer Lok needle had been used during the procedure. At approximately 1:00 PM, 4-year-old client accompanied with parents, received what was intended to be a dose of Pentacel (DTaP-IPV/Hib- LOT# UK422AA, Exp:06/2027). At approximately 3:15 PM, while preparing Pentacel for another client, RN  identified an inventory discrepancy and notified RN . During review of the vaccine preparation and administration, it was determined that the previously administered dose had not been prepared using the complete Pentacel components. Further review identified that the Pentacel Hib component had inadvertently been reconstituted using a Merck sterile diluent instead of the Pentacel DTaP-IPV liquid component. As a result, the client received the reconstituted Hib component but did not receive the DTaP-IPV component of Pentacel. At approximately 3:15 PM, Nurse who vaccinated the client identified that the Pentacel DTaP-IPV component remained unused. Supervisor  was notified at 3:19pm of the medication/vaccine administration error. Upon notification, the Supervisor,  directed staff to initiate a medication consultation and to contact the clients parents/ guardian and the vaccine manufacturer for further guidance and recommendations regarding appropriate clinical follow-up up and vaccination. At 3:30 PHN Supervisor informed Manager, , about the incident and the steps that had already been taken to address the incident.  Staff Nurse  attempted to contact the client's parents/guardian at approximately 3:30 PM. There was no answer, and a callback number was provided. At approximately 3:45 PM, Staff Nurse contacted Sanofi Pasteur, the manufacturer of Pentacel, for guidance. Per the manufacturer's representative, the administered Pentacel dose was considered invalid/incomplete and required revaccination. Staff were advised that no adverse effects were expected based on the reported circumstances. Manufacturer case number 02987128 was provided. At approximately 4:04 PM, Staff Nurse  contacted the on-call physician, Dr, and reported the incident and the manufacturer's recommendations. Dr advised staff to follow the manufacturer's guidance and arrange for revaccination. At approximately 4:12 PM, the client's father returned the call and spoke with Staff Nurse . The father was informed that the Pentacel dose administered earlier that day was considered incomplete/invalid and that the child would require re-vaccination. The father reported that the child was doing well with no observed adverse effects at that time. He was advised to seek medical attention for any concerning symptoms and agreed to return with the child for re-vaccination.

Went to sleep that night and woke the next morning with vertigo.  the vertigo lasted only the morning and thru the day felt very off, a little dizzy and spoke to my general practitioner doctor who recommended some vertigo exercises.  I tried the exercises several times, rested and the next morning woke with an article occluding my vision in my right eye.  Called the Opthamology clinic and they recommended I go to the emergency room at my local hospital.  The admitting ER doctor sent me for a dye contrast and non contrast brain scan.  the brain scan looked normal, however he told me I have a mild concussion and the back of my head where I hit the floor was tender.  I did not remember falling or hitting the floor so I was unaware of the concussion until the ER visit.  It has taken almost 4 weeks to start feeling better.  I have had visits with my general practitioner, chiropractic visits, Accupunture visits and deep tissue work to help relieve the pain and symptoms.

Describe Event, Problem, or Product Use Error: This older man has a history of DVT and a life-threatening pulmonary embolism in 2009. No pro-coagulant tendency was found although it was noted that his son had a pulmonary embolism after extensive air travel. The patient has been on warfarin ever since, by his choice. He is extremely compliant with warfarin and has had therapeutic INRs nearly always(rare exceptions related to holding medication for medical procedures, such as colonoscopy), usually 2.4-2.6, in all that time. He is not a smoker and has no other pulmonary history. He had a Moderna COVID-19 vaccine dose (#4 for him, no symptoms after the first 3 doses) on 11/19/2025. About 2 weeks later he noted new fatigue but no dyspnea, with drop in room air oxygen saturation from a baseline of 96-97% down to 92% with ambulation. He sought medical attention in May 2026. A CT angiogram revealed a new pulmonary embolism. His INR was 2.1 on that day, having been 2.6 a few days prior. He had a comprehensive hematology work up which did not reveal any pro-coagulant tendencies, and there was nothing in the history to suggest any factor which is known to provoke DVT or PE, such as airplane travel or recent surgery or immobilization. His cardiac echo showed mild right ventricular dilatation but no other abnormality. He was switched from warfarin to Eliquis with improvement in symptoms and with his O2 saturation back to baseline over several weeks. A repeat cardiac echo result is pending at this time. My concern is that COVID-19 infection is known to be associated with thromboses, and there have been reports of miscarriage after COVID-19 mRNA vaccination; I do not know the mechanism for miscarriage in these cases but it is plausible that a pro-coagulant effect could be at play. I have not seen other reports of unprovoked DVT or pulmonary embolism after mRNA COVID 19 vaccine, but I am concerned that this unprovoked pulmonary embolism occurring while therapeutically anticoagulated with warfarin could have occurred from the immunologic reaction to the COVID mRNA vaccination.
LAB_DATA: INR 29-May-2026 2.1; CT ANGIOGRAM OF THE CHEST 29-May-2026 pulmonary embolism; CARDIAC ECHO 28-May-2026 mild RV dilataion
HISTORY: Allergic to cephalexin only. Nonsmoker. Alcohol use 1 drink 5 times a week. No liver, kidney, cardiac, or pulmonary history except as above. He has hyperprolactinemia without a pituitary adenoma, and takes cabergoline 0.25 mg weekly with a low normal prolactin level. Warfarin was the only other medication at the time of the event.

SYMPTOM_TEXT: Describe Event, Problem, or Product Use Error: The nurse was administering Menveo and MenB vaccines. During administration of the MenB vaccine in the right arm, vaccine leaked from the clear plastic syringe top when pressure was applied to the plunger. The nurse immediately stopped the administration and informed the patient that the vaccine was not entering the arm. The nurse verified that the needle connection was secure and attempted administration again, but the vaccine again leaked from the syringe and sprayed away from the injection site. The nurse informed the patient and parent that the dose was unlikely to have been administered and consulted the provider and pharmacy regarding next steps. Based on the assessment, it was recommended that the dose be repeated. A CRM was submitted for the original lot due to concern for a potentially defective syringe or product. The original MenB vaccine was lot P794L (exp. 8/31/2028, GSK). A replacement dose was administered using lot 29HS7 (exp. 03/31/2029, GSK), and the administration was documented in the medical record. The original lot was removed from use and placed in the vaccine refrigerator with instructions not to use pending further evaluation. The nurse explained the situation and recommendation to repeat the vaccine to the parent, including concerns regarding a possible defective syringe. The parent verbalized understanding and agreed with the plan. The replacement MenB vaccine was successfully administered in the right deltoid.

SYMPTOM_TEXT: Received first dose of Twinrix (hepatitis A/hepatitis B vaccine) in left arm on Friday, August 14, 2026 at approximately 11:30 AM. I felt well prior to vaccination. The injection site bled more than I had previously experienced after vaccination; vaccinator asked whether I was taking blood thinners. I was not.  Later that evening/overnight, I developed significant pain predominantly on the left side of my body, including the left arm, neck, back and buttock, along with marked fatigue and intermittent fever. By Saturday morning, the pain was severe enough that walking and lifting my head were very difficult because of pain. I remained mostly in bed and was unable to attend a previously planned family college graduation event because of the severity of the symptoms. The pain and fatigue were significant enough that I did not eat until approximately 4 PM. I developed a severe headache primarily behind my left eye and intermittent numbness/heaviness on the left side of my face. I also experienced approximately 4–5 episodes of burning/pain with urination. I had no urinary symptoms before vaccination. I took two ibuprofen at approximately 3 PM, after which the pain improved substantially. Sleeping remained extremely uncomfortable Saturday night.  By Sunday, I no longer had urinary symptoms and the severe pain had improved; however, residual left arm, neck and lower-back pain remained. I noticed mild swelling of the left side of my face, particularly around the eye and cheek. The facial swelling subsequently resolved.  I was evaluated by telehealth by my PCP on Monday, August 17. PCP advised me not to receive additional Twinrix doses and ordered coagulation testing because of the bleeding at the injection site. I notified my Neurologist because I have a history of four episodes of Bell's palsy affecting the left side and am currently undergoing neurological evaluation.  Beginning Tuesday, August 18, I developed intermittent muscle spasms/twitching involving my left bicep, neck and left thigh. I also experienced heaviness on the left side of my face.  As of Wednesday, August 19, I am substantially improved but have not completely recovered. I continue to experience intermittent muscle spasms/twitching involving the left bicep, neck and left thigh, discomfort near the left elbow when extending my arm, residual fatigue and minimal lower-back discomfort. Left-arm discomfort continues to interfere with sleep, and I am using a pillow to elevate/support the arm at night. Facial swelling has resolved, and the sensation of left-sided facial heaviness experienced Tuesday has improved.
OTHER_MEDS: Ferrous Sulfate EC 324 MG, Fexofenadine Hydrochloride 180 MG, Amlodipine 5 MG, Hydrochlorothiazide 12.5 MG, Magnesium Glycinate 120 MG, Flonase Sensimist 27.5 MCG

Patient presents with adverse reaction to HPV vaccine #2 administered 3 weeks ago, consistent with deltoid tendon inflammation secondary to traumatic vaccine administration. The injection site appears positioned high, likely involving the deltoid tendon, and the described administration technique (rapid needle insertion, fast injection, angled withdrawal) suggests mechanical trauma to the tendon. Physical examination confirms localized induration and tenderness consistent with tendon inflammation. This represents a reportable adverse vaccine reaction requiring VAERS documentation. The 3-week delay between vaccination and symptom worsening is atypical but not inconsistent with tendon inflammation. Recent onset of systemic symptoms (chills, fatigue, malaise) occurring 3 weeks post-vaccination is difficult to attribute directly to the vaccine given the prolonged timeline. Differential considerations include concurrent viral illness versus delayed inflammatory response, though the temporal relationship makes direct causation uncertain.

My feet are constantly in pain. They hurt when wearing even (brand name withheld) shoes. The pads of my feet are very sensitive. I've been looked at by doctors, pediatrists, chiropractors, Foot and ankle doctors........I got x-rays to see if my backbone was messing with my nerves. SIRVA Injury Timeline  08/11/26 (Tuesday)   Vaccine Administration  11:03 AM: Received vaccine injection in the left upper arm. Immediately upon injection, I experienced excruciating burning pain. The nurse did not squeeze or otherwise locate the deltoid muscle before administering the injection. While I was crying from the pain, the nurse commented to my mother,  Some kids are just sensitive.   I attempted arm swings for approximately 15 minutes afterward, as instructed, to encourage movement and circulation.  Approximately 3 hours after vaccination: I remained in excruciating pain and was still crying despite taking 1,000 mg of Tylenol and using heated rice bags and ice packs. I have a very high pain tolerance and rarely cry because of medical procedures, making the severity of this pain unusual for me.  3:15 PM: Returned to Pediatrics and was evaluated by Dr. He noted no redness, swelling, or increased heat and recommended heat, ice, elevation, and a lower dose of Tylenol (400 mg).  During the visit, the comment  Well, we won't give you any narcotics  was made. My mother and I felt this was dismissive of my pain and that my symptoms were not being taken seriously. We had not requested narcotics, making the comment unprompted.  08/12/26 (Wednesday)   Urgent Care  I continued to experience significant pain with limited movement of my left arm. I went to urgent care and was told that the injection appeared to have potentially affected a ligament or tendon. I was advised to see an orthopedist if the pain persisted through Friday.  I was given a sling because I was holding my arm against my side to avoid jostling it. Steroid injections were offered, but I declined after being informed of potential effects.  As I was leaving, a nurse commented that they had never seen a vaccine administered that high and that the situation was  crazy.   I used the sling for that day only and began attempting pendulum exercises to maintain movement and encourage circulation.  08/13/26 (Thursday)  Pain began to decrease. Because the pain was less severe, I was able to raise my arm higher by pushing through the remaining pain.  08/14/26 (Friday)   Orthopedic Evaluation  Pain had decreased to approximately 3/10, but significant movement limitations remained. I could raise my arm, but at a certain point the movement became increasingly difficult, described as feeling as though  rocks were on top of my arm.  At that point, I could no longer push my arm higher.  I followed the urgent-care referral and was evaluated by an orthopedist. I was prescribed two anti-inflammatory medications and instructed to continue physical therapy.  The first medication prescribed was methylprednisolone. After completing nearly the entire course, I did not notice significant improvement. I was instructed to begin diclofenac after completing the methylprednisolone and to follow up after that course of treatment.  Steroid injections were discussed again as a potential option if conservative treatment did not improve my symptoms.  Current Status   08/20/26  I am now 9 days after the injection and continue to experience constant left shoulder pain and limited mobility. Pain increases with certain movements and when lifting or carrying objects.  My arm has also begun making popping noises and experiencing sensations of subluxation/instability, which I had never experienced before the vaccination.  My medical chart now officially documents the following diagnoses:  Acute pain of left shoulder Adverse effect of injectable substance Shoulder injury related to vaccine administration (SIRVA)  I am continuing treatment and monitoring my symptoms, including physical therapy and the prescribed anti-inflammatory medications. I cannot tie my hairback and it is limiting my life.
LAB_DATA: No imaging or specialized diagnostic testing has been performed to date. Evaluations have consisted of physical examinations and assessments of my symptoms and range of motion.  On 08/14/26, the orthopedist evaluated my left shoulder, including testing my range of motion. Based on the history of immediate pain following vaccine administration, the location and severity of the pain, and the resulting limitation in shoulder movement, the orthopedist diagnosed Shoulder Injury Related to Vaccine Administration (SIRVA).  I was informed that an MRI or ultrasound could be performed in the future if clinically indicated. However, I was told that imaging was not currently necessary to establish the SIRVA diagnosis and would result in an additional cost while likely not changing the current treatment plan. Therefore, no imaging has been performed at this time. I have been told there is a possibility this could be lifelong.

I had no prior history of migraine or debilitating headaches prior to vaccination.  On January 12, 2012, I received the Td vaccine. Approximately 6 hours post-vaccination, I experienced the sudden onset of a severe, debilitating migraine headache. Unlike previous occasional mild headaches, this event was characterized by throbbing pain, light sensitivity, and nausea. Despite standard abortive treatments (e.g., triptans, NSAIDs), the headache persisted. Over the subsequent 6 years, I experienced frequent, recurrent, and debilitating migraine attacks occurring [6 days per month]. These attacks are prostrating, requiring the patient to lie down in a dark room and resulting in significant loss of function. The chronic nature of this condition represents a distinct change from my baseline health status prior to January 12, 2012. The temporal association between the vaccination and the onset of this chronic, refractory migraine disorder is notable.

The intense immune response reactivated dormant Varicella Zoster in the eyes tissue. The patient went to urgent care who sent to emergency room, there was no ophthalmologist. Saw an ophthalmologist on day 4 and there was no shingles present in eye, so steroid and dilation drops were prescribed.  On day 5 showed some improvement with pain and light sensitivity and on day 6 started fine but then pain started again, on Days 7 and 8 (weekend) there was intense pain and light sensitivity, blurry vision continued with the addition of a milky white haze.  Got into ophthalmology on day 9, inflammation of cornea had doubled with severe pain, light sensitivity, and blurred vision.  The Hutchinson's sign was noted on the tip of the nose.  They increased the dosage on the steroid drops and started an oral anti-viral, day 10 showed much improvement.  No pain or light sensitivity, but blurry white hazy vision continued.  Saw ophthalmologist on day 11, eye itself showed decreased inflammation (hence no pain or light sensitive), but cornea still very inflamed, even more so than day 10 (hence blurry milky white vision).  They added a prescription of oral steroids.; Sender's Comments: Uveitis and Ophthalmic herpes zoster, less than a day after vaccination with 2nd dose of Shingrix and Shingrix PRE-FILLED SYRINGE DEVICE in a 53-year-old female patient. She also developed significant hematologic and coagulation abnormalities, including thrombocytopenia, markedly elevated D-dimer, decreased fibrinogen, prolonged PT/aPTT and INR, and decreased platelet function. She developed severe peripheral ischemia with cold/mottled extremities and absent distal pulses.  Her clinical course progressed to severe metabolic and lactic acidosis, acute kidney injury with minimal urine output requiring CRRT, neurologic injury/global cerebral ischemia following cardiac arrest, and encephalopathy/diffuse brain dysfunction. She was treated with ECMO, anticoagulation, CRRT, remdesivir, corticosteroids, tocilizumab, antibiotics, and other intensive supportive therapies. Despite treatment, she developed progressive multiorgan failure. Life support was withdrawn and patient died on 08/06/2022.  The adverse event occurred 22 days after the second Pfizer COVID-19 vaccine dose. She also had laboratory-confirmed acute COVID-19 infection at the time of her deterioration. This report is intended to document the complete clinical course and objective findings for evaluation of the adverse event and its possible relationship to vaccination.

One of my immunizing technicians was giving the flu vaccine to a patient and a minute after administering it she get me and let me know the patient was having a reaction. My technician let me know that the patient's arm was breaking out into bumps and red and irritated. When I came into the room a minute or less after the patient's arm had a couple of bumps quickly fading but no redness. In addition, the patient complained of having lightheadedness to the point that she had to close her eyes. Upon further investigation, my tech and the patient informed me that her biceps muscle had twitched when she administered the vaccine. Her family members were in the room at the same time and noticed the redness and looked like the vaccine was moving down the patient's arm. The patient said that she felt the vaccine go into her arm and down the arm and up her neck. After about 5 minutes after receiving the flu vaccine she developed a metallic taste in her mouth. When I looked over her arm and the vaccine site about 5 to 10 minutes later, she said she had a chills/prickly feeling around the injection site and could feel the vaccine moving. We had the patient sit in the chair in the immunization room for 15 to 20 minutes after receiving the vaccine. The lightheadedness improved and before the patient left she felt a lot better. We put a call into the patient's PCP to inform them of what happened and the patient's husband drove her home;

She received the Boostrix tdap in her right arm at approximately 0800 8/25/26 and subsequently developed a new diffuse rash involving the arms and legs and also the chest and abdomen. She has had prior tetanus vaccinations without similar reactions, though it has been a long time since the last one.   She denies pruritus, shortness of breath, wheezing, nausea, vomiting, facial or lip involvement, and oral lesions. She denies recent travel.   She received benadryl and pepcid at approximately 1400 today. She denies any new medications or exposures. No chest pain or shortness of breath. On arrival to ED, patient is hemodynamically stable and resting comfortably on room air. Physical exam is notable for diffuse blanchable macular rash throughout body, sparing face and mucosa.    Differential diagnosis includes, but is not limited to, allergic reaction, anaphylaxis, hypersensitivity reaction, SJS, DRESS, viral xanthem   Low concern for anaphylaxis as patient does not have multi-system involvement. Patient is well-appearing and there is no evidence of skin sloughing that would be concerning for SJS. Similarly, no fever or systemic involvement that would be worrisome for DRESS. Patient was in her normal state of health without infectious symptoms so I doubt viral xanthem.    Given exposure to Tdap booster, I am concerned for allergic reaction vs. Hypersensitivity reaction to the vaccine. She was given benadryl and pepcid in triage without improvement in symptoms. However, patient denies any pruritus and is well appearing so I suspect self-limiting process and she was cleared for discharge home. Instructed patient to avoid boostrix tdap in the future given this reaction.

In July 2020, eight months before the index event patient presented to the Emergency Department (ED) with epigastric and right upper quadrant abdominal pain accompanied by symptoms suggestive of a urinary tract infection (UTI). She had no prior history of COVID-19 infection. COVID-19 vaccination was not yet available at the time of this hospitalization.  In January/February 2021, the patient received the first dose of the Moderna mRNA 1273 (Spikevax) COVID-19 vaccine. On 16-Mar-2021, she received the second dose. Within 24 h, on 17 March 2021, she presented to the ED with acute-onset abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, headaches, and dizziness. The pain did not improve with analgesic medication. She also reported dysuria.  Patient admitted on 18-Mar-2021 (hospitalization Day 0). Hypercalcemia management was initiated on Day 0 with intravenous (IV) normal saline hydration and a single dose of pamidronate disodium 60 mg IV. Despite initial treatment, serum calcium peaked at 17.4 mg/dL on Day 1, after which IV furosemide was added. Serum calcium normalized on Day 8 without myeloma-directed treatment.  During the hospitalization, the patient also developed hyperammonemic encephalopathy which was treated with lactulose and resolved in parallel with the improvement in renal function and hypercalcemia. On Day 11, bone marrow sampling from the right iliac crest was obtained for hematopathology consultation. FISH and molecular studies were not performed.  Based on the integration of all clinical, laboratory, histopathological, immunophenotypic, and cytogenetic findings, a final diagnosis of newly diagnosed biclonal IgA MM with aberrant expression of multiple high-risk markers, including CD33, CD43, OCT-2, c-MYC, and gain of chromosome 1q, was rendered.  On Day 12, hemoglobin had decreased and two units of packed red blood cells (PRBCs) were transfused. Low-dose dexamethasone phosphate 8 mg IV was initiated on Day 11 as part of the discharge preparation regimen, followed by 4 mg IV on Day 12. The patient was discharged on Day 13 and post-transfusion Hgb of 10.3 g/dL. However, normocytic anemia persisted. Notably, there was no documentation that myeloma-directed systemic therapy was initiated at any point during the hospitalization or at discharge. After discharge, the patient was lost to hematology-oncology follow-up.  In December 2021, nine months after the MM diagnosis, the patient returned to the ED with a one-month history of abdominal pain, vomiting, and diarrhea. She was diagnosed with acute gastritis and acute cystitis and treated with famotidine and ciprofloxacin. Review of her medication history confirmed that no myeloma-directed therapy had been received after her March 2021 discharge. She was noted to be taking Gabapentin (dosage not documented), prescribed following the index hospitalization. The continued absence of osteolytic lesions across all three time points (July 2020, March 2021, and December 2021), despite the confirmed diagnosis of high-risk MM, represents a diagnostically unusual and clinically significant finding in this case.  The author stated temporal proximity of the hypercalcemic crisis to the second dose of the Moderna mRNA 1273 vaccine suggested a plausible precipitating role for the vaccine-induced inflammatory response without implying causation and without ruling out coincidence. During the original appointment, I had provided the parent with information regarding the App. During the follow-up conversation, I informed the parent that the patient?s vaccine history had been updated in the state system and encouraged her to utilize the App and provide a copy of the updated vaccine record to the child?s school. Proximal Humerus Osteomyelitis After Influenza Vaccination Administration; Shoulder Injury Related to Vaccine Administration (SIRVA); the patient described prolonged bleeding at the injection site; accidental intraosseous administration/vaccination was suspected to have been given above or close to the deltoid tendon; This serious case was reported in a literature article and described the occurrence of acute osteomyelitis in a 55-year-old female patient who received Flu Seasonal QIV Dresden (Influenza vaccine Quadrivalent unspecified season) solution for injection for prophalaxis. Literature Reference: Concurrent medical conditions included penetrating trauma. Additional patient notes included Patient denied preceding injury, fever, or chills and no abscess, and rotator cuff tendinosis without focal tear.   On an unknown date, the patient received Influenza vaccine Quadrivalent unspecified season (left deltoid). On an unknown date, 3 months after receiving Influenza vaccine Quadrivalent unspecified season, the patient experienced acute osteomyelitis (Verbatim: Proximal Humerus Osteomyelitis After Influenza Vaccination Administration) (serious criteria GSK medically significant), shoulder injury related to vaccine administration (Verbatim: Shoulder Injury Related to Vaccine Administration (SIRVA)) (serious criteria clinically significant/intervention required), vaccination site hemorrhage (Verbatim: the patient described prolonged bleeding at the injection site) and vaccine administered at inappropriate site (Verbatim: accidental intraosseous administration/vaccination was suspected to have been given above or close to the deltoid tendon). The patient was treated with doxycycline and levofloxacin (Levaquin). The outcome of the acute osteomyelitis, shoulder injury related to vaccine administration and vaccination site hemorrhage were resolved and the outcome of the vaccine administered at inappropriate site was not applicable.   The reporter considered the acute osteomyelitis, shoulder injury related to vaccine administration and vaccination site hemorrhage to be related to Influenza vaccine Quadrivalent unspecified season.  The company considered the acute osteomyelitis and shoulder injury related to vaccine administration to be unrelated to Influenza vaccine Quadrivalent unspecified season. The company considered the vaccination site hemorrhage to be related to Influenza vaccine Quadrivalent unspecified season.   Additional Information: GSK Receipt date 24-AUG-2026 Author reported that patient with a normal medical history and no predisposing risk factors for infection presented with 3 months of left shoulder pain after receiving an influenza quad (PF) vaccine. When the deltoid vaccine was administered, the patient described prolonged bleeding at the injection site. The patient presented to her primary care physician, and after little improvement from ice and range of motion exercises, a noncontrast magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the left shoulder was ordered. The vaccination was suspected to have been given above or close to the deltoid tendon, with an initial leading diagnosis of shoulder injury related to vaccine administration (SIRVA). Arriving in clinic the patient reported sharp left posterolateral shoulder pain radiating to the elbow and hand. On examination Patient demonstrated left posterolateral shoulder tenderness, 160 forward flexion of the left shoulder compared with 170 on the right, external rotation to 60 on the left and 80 on the right, and internal rotation to T12 bilaterally. Patient had diminished strength, including 2/5 strength with external rotation, 41/5 strength with belly press, and 4/5 strength with forward flexion. Tingling was present in the left palm, but sensation was otherwise intact. Noncontrast magnetic resonance imaging of the left shoulder showed focal marrow edema within the posterior humeral head with overlying soft tissue and periosteal edema. Given the patient history of penetrating trauma and the distinct humeral head marrow and periosteal edema, osteomyelitis was considered the most likely diagnosis An infection work-up was done. Complete blood count showed a marginally low white blood cell of 3.98 (4.00 to 10.00 x10E3 uL), C-reactive protein less than 1.0 mg/L (greater than equal to 10.0 mg/L), and erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 3 mm/hr (0 to 20 mm/hr). An infectious disease consult advised a trial of empirical antibiotics with gram positive and gram-negative coverage; a biopsy was not recommended at this time. The patient underwent a 6-week course of doxycycline and levaquin antibiotics through the peripherally inserted central catheter (PICC) line. Although the patient experienced some improvement Patient continued to have decreased shoulder motion and was referred to physical therapy. A repeat magnetic resonance imaging was ordered to evaluate the rotator cuff and for ongoing evidence of osteomyelitis. Repeat MRI with and without contrast showed interval resolution of marrow edema pattern corresponding to the posterior aspect of the proximal humerus with no evidence to suggest proximal humerus osteomyelitis. Moderate shoulder joint synovial enhancement was consistent with synovitis and no evidence of a rotator cuff tear. Ultimately the patient elected to proceed with surgery for ongoing adhesive capsulitis which included arthroscopic debridement and evaluation of the left shoulder with culture and manipulation under anesthesia and possible capsular release. Patient responded well to a 6-week course of IV antibiotics and the repeat MRI did not show signs of osteomyelitis open cultures and bone biopsy were not obtained. The patient was taken to the operating room and placed in a beach chair position. After the left upper extremity was sterilely prepped and draped, an aspiration was done and sanguinous fluid was sent for cultures. On arthroscopic evaluation, early grade 1 or 2 wear of the superior aspect of the humeral head was noted, along with a considerable amount of synovitis within the shoulder joint and no signs of labrum or rotator cuff tearing. The shoulder was debrided and synovial tissue was sent for cultures. Manipulation under anesthesia partially improved her passive motion and a capsular release improved her motion to near normal. Prophy lactic antibiotics were administered after all cultures were obtained. Incisions were closed, and the patient was transferred to the recovery room. Intraoperative tissue cultures sent for aerobic and anaerobic testing were negative after 1 week of incubation. Physical therapy began 5 days postoperatively to start active and passive range of motion and the sling was discontinued soon after surgery. At the patient's most recent clinical follow-up over 1 year after her influenza vaccine patient had regained full range of motion equal to her contralateral shoulder. Patient regained full rotator cuff strength except for slightly diminished strength in the subscapularis (41/5 strength with belly press) similar to initial examination. The case we have presented seeks to inform clinicians about the potential risk of osteomyelitis after accidental intraosseous administration of a flu vaccine. After several months of ongoing shoulder pain and decreased motion, the patient was initially suspected to have shoulder injury related to vaccine administration. After little improvement with conservative management and an magnetic resonance imaging with focal marrow and periosteal edema of the humeral head, patient underwent a 6-week course of IV antibiotics for suspected osteomyelitis. Repeat magnetic resonance imaging with and without contrast showed interval resolution of marrow edema pattern corresponding to the posterior aspect of the proximal humerus. The patient proceeded with surgery to treat residual adhesive capsulitis, including arthroscopic debridement and evaluation of the left shoulder with culture, manipulation under anesthesia, and capsular release. Intraoperative aerobic and anaerobic cultures were negative. Ultimately, patient made a full recovery with normal motion and strength by her 1-year postoperative evaluation. Case lacks further information on medical history, and laboratory data. Based on the available information a possible causality that the event was caused by the GSK product cannot be ascertained. Further follow up information has been sought. Shoulder injury related to vaccine administration, 3 months after vaccination with Influenza vaccine Quadrivalent in a 55-year-old female patient. Report is inconsistent with causal relation to the vaccine product, considering implausible time to onset and absence of biological plausibility.

The patient's relevant medical history and concomitant medications were not reported. The following information was reported: CEREBRAL THROMBOSIS (medically significant), outcome "unknown", described as "central nervous system thrombosis".  Clinical course: Clinical course: The coronavirus disease 2019 (Covid-19) pandemic caused by severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) stimulated the development of highly effective vaccines that were produced with unprecedented speed with the use of diverse technologies. No major safety warnings, other than rare cases of anaphylaxis, were reported in the initial trials, which involved tens of thousands of adults, and the risk of serious adverse effects has remained remarkably low after vaccination of more than 400 million people worldwide to date.1 It is not surprising, however, that new reports of adverse events have emerged as many additional people are vaccinated and follow-up is extended. For example, cases of immune thrombocytopenia and bleeding without thrombosis that were induced or revealed after exposure to the messenger RNA (mRNA) based vaccines produced by Moderna (mRNA-1273) and Pfizer-BioNTech (BNT162b2) have been reported. The Journal has now highlighted three independent descriptions of 39 persons with a newly described syndrome characterized by thrombosis and thrombocytopenia that developed 5 to 24 days after initial vaccination with ChAdOx1 nCoV-19 (AstraZeneca), a recombinant chimpanzee adenoviral vector encoding the spike protein of SARS-CoV-2.3-5 These persons were healthy or in medically stable condition, and very few were known to have had previous thrombosis or a preexisting prothrombotic condition. Most of the patients included in these reports were women younger than 50 years of age, some of whom were receiving estrogen-replacement therapy or oral contraceptives. A remarkably high percentage of the patients had thromboses at unusual sites specifically, cerebral venous sinus thrombosis or thrombosis in the portal, splanchnic, or hepatic veins. Other patients presented with deep venous thrombi, pulmonary emboli, or acute arterial thromboses. The median platelet counts at diagnosis were approximately 20,000 to 30,000 per cubic millimeter (range, approximately 10,000 to 110,000), but the rate of decline in platelet counts that preceded thrombosis is unknown. High levels of d-dimers and low levels of fibrinogen were common and suggest systemic activation of coagulation. Approximately 40% of the patients died, some from ischemic brain injury, superimposed hemorrhage, or both conditions, often after anticoagulation. This constellation of thrombosis and thrombocytopenia prompted consideration of heparin induced thrombocytopenia as the diagnosis. However, none of the patients had known exposure to heparin before the onset of illness. Although the pathogenesis of this syndrome of vaccine-induced immune thrombotic thrombocytopenia (VITT) is not yet clear, certain findings were consistent across the three studies. In almost every patient, high levels of antibodies to platelet factor 4 (PF4) polyanion complexes were identified by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA), as well by assays based on platelet activation, which, when tested, was enhanced by addition of PF4. In contrast to heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, however, binding of antibody to PF4 occurred in the absence of heparin. This serologic pattern mirrors findings in patients with atypical or autoimmune heparin induced thrombocytopenia, in whom thrombi develop in the absence of known previous exposure to heparin,6 but the distribution of thrombi in patients with that condition clearly differs from that in patients with VITT. On the basis of these reports, the diagnosis of VITT should be confirmed with an approved PF4 ELISA. Reliance cannot be placed on the rapid assays that are often used to detect heparin-induced thrombocytopenia unless they have been validated to make or to rule out a diagnosis of VITT, given the potential differences in antigenic target or sensitivity. The limited information available relating to management suggests that intravenous immune globulin and high-dose glucocorticoids can im prove the platelet count within days, which may limit the risk of hemorrhagic transformation, especially when anticoagulation is instituted. Immune globulin impedes antibody-mediated platelet clearance and may down-regulate platelet activation by immune complexes by blocking platelet FcR?IIA receptors, as in heparin-induced thrombocytopenia.7 Although the condition in several patients apparently improved when they were given low-molecular-weight heparin, it seems prudent to choose from among the nonheparin antithrombotic agents that are used to treat heparin-induced thrombocytopenia while the risk of bleeding is being mitigated.8 We expect that the high mortality rate associated with VITT will decrease with earlier recognition and improved intervention. No thrombotic signal was detected in clinical trials leading to the approval of the ChAdOx1 nCoV-19 vaccine,9 which has now been administered to 34 million people worldwide. The incidence of VITT, as initially estimated, is perhaps 1 case per 100,000 exposures. This should be considered in the context of the incidence of cerebral venous sinus thrombosis in the general population (estimated at 0.22 to 1.57 cases per 100,000 per year). The initial focus of these reports may reflect a propensity to study patients with severe thrombosis occurring in unusual locations, and a more complete picture of thrombotic complications is likely to emerge over time. More information on potential risk factors other than young age and female sex is needed. Also needed are data on the prevalence and titer of anti-PF4 related antibodies in all vaccine recipients, especially those who had thrombosis at sites other than those commonly reported to date among patients with VITT, in order to apply Bayesian analyses to estimate disease probability on the basis of both clinical features and antibody titer in optimized assays. This may be complicated to achieve, because many cases of thrombosis that occur after vaccination are unlikely to be directly provoked by this exposure. Better understanding of how the vaccine induces these platelet-activating antibodies might also provide insight into the duration of antigen exposure and the risk of reoccurrence of thrombosis, which will inform the need for extended anticoagulation and might lead to improvements in vaccine design. Additional cases have now been reported to the RA, including at least 169 possible cases of cerebral venous sinus thrombosis and 53 possible cases of splanchnic vein thrombosis among 34 million recipients of the ChAdOx1 nCoV-19 vaccine, 35 possible cases of central nervous system thrombosis among 54 million recipients of the Pfizer-BioNTech mRNA vaccine, and 5 possible (but unvetted) cases of cerebral venous sinus thrombosis among 4 million recipients of the Moderna mRNA vaccine. Six possible cases of cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (with or without splanchnic vein thrombosis) have been reported among the more than 7 million recipients of the Johnson & Johnson/Janssen Ad26.COV2.S adenoviral vector vaccine. It must be emphasized that not all of these case reports have been subject to rigorous central review, nor have results of tests for anti-PF4 antibodies been reported; however, these numbers may be underestimates, since reporting is voluntary. Nevertheless, they clearly indicate the need for maintaining a high level of concern when patients present with central nervous system or abdominal symptoms after receiving any SARSCoV-2 vaccine. These new observations also raise important scientific questions with clinical implications. What component or components of the vaccine (adenoviral sequence, spike protein, or other component) elicit a new (or recall) response to a seemingly unrelated host protein, PF4? Why does the complication appear to be more prevalent after exposure to one particular adenoviral vector? What is the risk after revaccination? How do VITT antibodies compare with the anti-PF4-related antibodies that are present after SARSCoV-2 infection, which have been described in patients who were suspected to have heparin induced thrombocytopenia?10-12 Is PF4 a bystander component within an immune complex that activates platelets, or does it contribute directly to clot propagation? Does the atypical distribution of thrombi relate to antigen localization or vascular response? Is thrombosis propagated along vascular and hematopoietic surfaces that release diverse anionic cofactors, as in heparin-induced thrombocytopenia? In one preliminary report, the investigators reported that antibodies to PF4 do not cross-react with the spike protein.13 De tailed study of anti-PF4 antibodies after natural infection and in recipients of each of the SARSCoV-2 vaccines may provide insight into the risk of VITT and into the pathophysiological mechanisms underlying the condition. A note of caution: although anti-PF4-polyanion antibodies are common for example, they are detected in 25 to 50% of patients after cardiovascular surgery heparin-induced thrombocytopenia is not, and only in rare cases does cerebral venous sinus thrombosis or thrombi in abdominal vessels develop in patients with heparin-induced thrombocytopenia. This suggests that our understanding of the pathogenesis of VITT is incomplete, and the usefulness of measuring pathogenic anti-PF4-related antibodies in all vaccine recipients has not been established. To close the loop, the next step should be a direct demonstration that the anti-PF4 antibodies described here cause thrombosis and thrombocytopenia in an in vivo model. The very low prevalence of this complication of vaccination, however severe, relative to the benefits of preventing Covid-19 (a condition with 1 to 2% mortality and potential long-term sequelae) must be emphasized. As of 09Apr2021, at least five countries had instituted limitations primarily based on age on which patients should receive the ChAdOx1 nCoV-19 vaccine, and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the Food and Drug Administration have put a temporary hold on administration of the Johnson & Johnson/Janssen vaccine. The questions of whether certain populations can be identified as more suitable candidates for one or another vaccine and who and how to monitor for this rare potential complication will require additional study. In almost every patient, high levels of antibodies to platelet factor 4 (PF4)–polyanion complexes were identified by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA), as well by assays based on platelet activation, which, when tested, was enhanced by addition of PF4. In contrast to heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, however, binding of antibody to PF4 occurred in the absence of heparin. This serologic pattern mirrors findings in patients with "atypical" or "autoimmune" heparininduced thrombocytopenia, in whom thrombi develop in the absence of known previous exposure to heparin, but the distribution of thrombi in patients with that condition clearly differs from that in patients with VITT. On the basis of these reports, the diagnosis of VITT should be confirmed with an approved PF4 ELISA. Privacy cannot be placed on the rapid assays that are often used to detect heparin-induced thrombocytopenia unless they have been validated to make or to rule out a diagnosis of VITT, given the potential differences in antigenic target or sensitivity. The limited information available relating to management suggests that intravenous immune globulin and high-dose glucocorticoids can improve the platelet count within days, which may limit the risk of hemorrhagic transformation, especially when anticoagulation is instituted. Immune globulin impedes antibody-mediated platelet clearance and may down-regulate platelet activation by immune complexes by blocking platelet FcR?IIA receptors, as in heparin-induced thrombocytopenia. Although the condition in several patients apparently improved when they were given low-molecular-weight heparin, it seems prudent to choose from among the no heparin antithrombotic agents that are used to treat heparin-induced thrombocytopenia while the risk of bleeding is being mitigated. We expect that the high mortality rate associated with VITT will decrease with earlier recognition and improved intervention. No thrombotic signal was detected in clinical trials leading to the approval of the ChAdOx1 nCoV-19 vaccine, which has now been administered to 34 million people worldwide. The incidence of VITT, as initially estimated, is perhaps 1 case per 100,000 exposures. This should be considered in the context of the incidence of cerebral venous sinus thrombosis in the general population (estimated at 0.22 to 1.57 cases per 100,000 per year). The initial focus of these reports may reflect a propensity to study patients with severe thrombosis occurring in unusual locations, and a more complete picture of thrombotic complications is likely to emerge over time. More information on potential risk factors other than young age and female sex is needed. Also needed are data on the prevalence and titer of anti-PF4–related antibodies in all vaccine recipients, especially those who had thrombosis at sites other than those commonly reported to date among patients with VITT, in order to apply Bayesian analyses to estimate disease probability on the basis of both clinical features and antibody titer in optimized assays. This may be complicated to achieve, because many cases of thrombosis that occur after vaccination are unlikely to be directly provoked by this exposure. Better understanding of how the vaccine induces these platelet-activating antibodies might also provide insight into the duration of antigen exposure and the risk of reoccurrence of thrombosis, which will inform the need for extended anticoagulation and might lead to improvements in vaccine design. Additional cases have now been reported to the withheld, including at least 169 possible cases of cerebral venous sinus thrombosis and 53 possible cases of splanchnic vein thrombosis among 34 million recipients of the ChAdOx1 nCoV-19 vaccine, 35 possible cases of central nervous system thrombosis among 54 million recipients of the Pfizer–BioNTech mRNA vaccine, and 5 possible (but unvetted) cases of cerebral venous sinus thrombosis among 4 million recipients of the Moderna mRNA vaccine. Six possible cases of cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (with or without splanchnic vein thrombosis) have been reported among the more than 7 million recipients of the withheld Ad26.COV2.S adenoviral vector vaccine. It must be emphasized that not all of these case reports have been subject to rigorous central review, nor have results of tests for anti-PF4 antibodies been reported; however, these numbers may be underestimates, since reporting is voluntary. Nevertheless, they clearly indicate the need for maintaining a high level of concern when patients present with central nervous system or abdominal symptoms after receiving any SARSCoV- 2 vaccine. These new observations also raise important scientific questions with clinical implications. What component or components of the vaccine (adenoviral sequence, spike protein, or other component) elicit a new (or recall) response to a seemingly unrelated host protein, PF4? Why does the complication appear to be more prevalent after exposure to one particular adenoviral vector? What is the risk after revaccination? How do VITT antibodies compare with the anti-PF4-related antibodies that are present after SARSCoV-2 infection, which have been described in patients who were suspected to have heparin induced thrombocytopenia? Is PF4 a bystander component within an immune complex that activates platelets, or does it contribute directly to clot propagation? Does the atypical distribution of thrombi relate to antigen localization or vascular response? Is thrombosis propagated along vascular and hematopoietic surfaces that release diverse anionic cofactors, as in heparin-induced thrombocytopenia? In one preliminary report, the investigators reported that antibodies to PF4 do not cross-react with the spike protein. These new observations tailed study of anti-PF4 antibodies after natural infection and in recipients of each of the SARSCoV- 2 vaccines may provide insight into the risk of VITT and into the pathophysiological mechanisms underlying the condition. A note of caution: although anti-PF4-polyanion antibodies are common for example, they are detected in 25 to 50% of patients after cardiovascular surgery heparin-induced thrombocytopenia is not, and only in rare cases does cerebral venous sinus thrombosis or thrombi in abdominal vessels develop in patients with heparin-induced thrombocytopenia. This suggests that our understanding of the pathogenesis of VITT is incomplete, and the usefulness of measuring pathogenic anti-PF4-related antibodies in all vaccine recipients has not been established. To close the loop, the next step should be a direct demonstration that the anti-PF4 antibodies described here cause thrombosis and thrombocytopenia in an in vivo model. The very low prevalence of this complication of vaccination, however severe, relative to the benefits of preventing Covid-19 (a condition with 1 to 2% mortality and potential long-term sequelae) must be emphasized. As of 9Apr2021, at least five countries had instituted limitations- primarily based on age- on which patients should receive the ChAdOx1 nCoV-19 vaccine, and withheld and withheld have put a temporary hold on administration of the withheld. The questions of whether certain populations can be identified as more suitable candidates for one or another vaccine and who and how to monitor for this rare potential complication will require additional study. Pt presented to the pharmacy today asking about possible side effects of his vaccines. Pt got 2nd shingles and Flublok vaccines on Thurs, Aug 28. Pt states he worked outside in his field on Sunday cutting the grass with his zero-turn lawnmower. When he got off, he noticed some itching in his legs, primarily his thighs, and thought he'd gotten into red bugs or poison ivy. He bathed with a poison ivy soap thinking it would help with the itching. On Mon, Aug 31, pt stated he woke with large raised bumps on feet/legs that was spreading up his back and his hands are swollen. He said he didn't have any localized ADRs other than arm soreness. He denied localized fever/swelling/rash/hives around injection site and specifically stated the rash/raised bumps were on his legs with some between his shoulder blades and his hands were swollen and itching. He described the reaction as "coming and going and spreading through his body". All patients were treated with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), while seven (88 %) received colchicine, which was continued long-term in five cases. Corticosteroids were required in all eight (100 %) patients due to persistent or worsening symptoms. Corticosteroids were tapered off gradually, two (25 %) suffered side effects and four (50 %) patients experienced a recurrence during tapering. Six (75 %) patients were started on a weekly dose of rilonacept, an Interleukin-1 (IL- 1) blocker, and had complete resolution of symptoms. Two (33 %) experienced minor flares when the interval between the rilonacept dose was increased to every 3 and 4 weeks, with a resolution of symptoms when resuming weekly injections. All six (100 %) continue to be on weekly treatment at this time.  Conclusions: An association between vaccinations, including SARS-CoV2, and pericarditis has been long recognized. The authors herein report a group of cases of difficult-to-treat recurrent pericarditis. SARS-CoV2 vaccination- related pericarditis typically manifests with mild clinical signs in young male individuals, usually a few days after the second or third vaccine dose and is commonly characterized by a rapid and complete recovery. However, an initial episode of pericarditis may, in rare instances, trigger an autoinflammatory response in the pericardium that can last for months and years, and it may lead to serious and life-threatening complications like effusion, constriction, and tamponade. Independent of the initial insult, treatment requires interruption of the pro- inflammatory vicious cycle mediated by the inflammasome and IL-1. Viral proteins, i.e., SARS-CoV2 spike protein, are known to activate the inflammasome and induce the production of IL-1. Although uncommon, post-vaccination pericarditis can be recurrent and difficult to manage, with recurrence occurring in up to 21 % of cases. Prompt recognition and appropriate treatment of both initial and re lapsing episodes are essential to alleviate symptoms and prevent plications. Increased clinical awareness is crucial to identify patients at risk for more severe or persistent disease and to tailor therapy accordingly.; Sender's Comments: Based on known drug safety profile, there is reasonable possibility of causal association between the events pericarditis and disease recurrence and the suspect drug BNT162B2 NOS. SYMPTOM_TEXT: Approximately two minutes after vaccination, I noticed he had begun shutting his eyes and I asked how he was feeling, he said he felt like he needed to burp and that there was wind blowing in his ears. I provided him with 12OZ of water and a trashcan. He finished all the provided water and said he felt hot. The AC in the van was turned to a higher setting. I took his pulse ox it was 99% and his heart rate was 70bpm. After roughly 3 additional minutes, his teeth began to chatter and I asked if he felt cold and he said he didn't know if he was hot or cold. He said he was unable to control or stop the chattering and this continued for several minutes. He wanted to move to the floor of the van to try to lay down and during this time his jaw continued to chatter and his legs began tremoring. I spoke with the school nurse and we determined it was best to call 911 and escalate care. The patient requested to leave the van because he thought his tremors may be due to being in a small space and we escorted him to the school nurse's office to wait for EMS. He continued to experience tremors while waiting and when he left with EMS. His vitals signs were BP 118/70, HR 70, RR 18, O2 99% and he was responsive and aware throughout the encounter.

Diagnosis requires a =4x increase in two IgG titers two weeks apart, with the second sample drawn at 14-28 days of illness. SYMPTOM_TEXT: Recurrent influenza vaccine-induced cryoglobulinemic vasculitis; worsening bilateral lower leg rash starting as small circles growing into larger lesions; severe acute kidney injury; Hypocomplementemia; Leukocytoclastic vasculitis; CASE: An 83-year-old male with history of coronary artery disease, congestive heart failure and type II diabetes mellitus presented with four-days of worsening bilateral lower leg rash starting as small circles growing into larger lesions. Exam was notable for a non-blanchable, violaceous rash with irregular margins on the bilateral ankles. He was found to have acute kidney injury, elevated rheumatoid factor, hypocomplementemia (specifically C4), and skin biopsy showed leukocytoclastic vasculitis. Immunofixation showed monoclonal IgM and polyclonal IgG, confirming Type II cryoglobulinemia. He was administered a short course of steroids and rapidly improved. One year later, he presented with a similar appearing rash and severe acute kidney injury. Lab work up was identical, and he was found to have recurrence of his vasculitis. He was again initiated on steroids with rapid improvement. Further investigation found the patient had received the influenza vaccine just one week prior to both episodes with otherwise unrevealing evaluations for the cause of his recurrent vasculitis. IMPACT/DISCUSSION: Influenza vaccine-mediated mixed cryoglobulinemia type II alone is a rare adverse event. From this case, clinicians are encouraged to consider vaccine-induced vasculitis, especially when the work-up is otherwise negative for typical etiologies. While the exact pathophysiology of this mechanism remains unknown, this case offers clarity on the risk factors for the development of cryoglobulinemic vasculitis following vaccination. Based on available literature, patients with pre-existing cryoglobulinemic vasculitis, active peripheral neuropathy, or skin vasculitis appear to be the primary at-risk population for vaccine-induced disease relapse or exacerbation. The temporal association suggests vaccination may potentially trigger immune-mediated reactivation in susceptible patients with prior associated vasculitis. This association between influenza vaccine and cryoglobulinemic vasculitis, potentially with renal complications, highlights the importance of recognizing this connection for timely diagnosis and management. Due to the limited data related to vaccine-associated cryoglobulinemia, weighing individual risk factors, as part of clinical judgment, is essential to guiding vaccination decisions. CONCLUSION: Influenza vaccination-associated mixed cryoglobulinemia type II is a rare adverse event, documented only in a few isolated case reports. When evaluating patients presenting with purpura, vasculitis, or acute kidney injury following influenza vaccination, vaccine-induced cryoglobulinemic vasculitis can be considered after excluding more common etiologies, such as hepatitis infection, lymphoproliferative disorders, and systemic autoimmune diseases. While the safety profile for influenza vaccination is overall favorable, select populations with known risk factors may benefit from dedicated shared-decision making discussions.
